title: A wondrous recitation
hook: a group of jinn listened and said, we've heard a wondrous recitation (72:1–2)
carry: it guides to what is right

segments.voice: Yesterday: Nuh's last prayer, and your line, forgive me and my parents. Today, a surah with an unexpected audience.

Dawn, in a valley on the road to the market of 'Ukaz. A small group of travelers stop to pray, and one of them leads, reciting aloud. Nobody else is around, as far as they know. But someone is listening: a group of beings who had come searching for something else entirely, who stop, gather close, and hear the words to the end. Then they go home to their people and say: we've heard something wondrous. Surah seventy-two is named for them. Al-Jinn.

The surah begins with an instruction to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: say, it has been revealed to me that a group of the jinn listened. And they said, in Pickthall's translation: "Lo! we have heard a marvellous Qur'an." Marvelous is 'ajab in Arabic: wondrous, astonishing, something that makes you stop. Qur'an here means what it literally means: a recitation. The jinn, in Islamic belief, are real beings, created from smokeless fire, unseen by us, with free will like humans. Some believe, some don't. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, from Ibn 'Abbas, tells the setting. The jinn had noticed the sky had changed; they were being driven back from listening at the heavens, so they spread out across the earth to find out why. One group came upon the Prophet and his companions at a place called Nakhlah, praying the dawn prayer. They heard the recitation and said: this is what has come between us and the sky. One surprising detail: the verse says it was revealed to me that they listened. In Ibn 'Abbas's account, the Prophet didn't see them that morning; he learned about his audience afterward, through revelation. Then the jinn went back to their people, verse two: it guides to what is right, so we believe in it, and we will not set up anyone as partner to our Lord. Their response wasn't fear. It was wonder. They came looking for an explanation and found a recitation, and in verse two it's the recitation itself, guiding to what is right, that they say won them over.

If you can, play a recitation of the Qur'an quietly, any reciter, any surah, and just listen, even if you don't understand the Arabic. If you'd rather not, close your eyes and listen to whatever is around you, traffic, wind, your own breath, as if you'd never heard it before. Notice the moment something sounds new.
'Ajab. In 72:1 a group of jinn hear the Qur'an at dawn and call it wondrous, 'ajab, astonishing enough to make them stop and listen. Today's word.
Your line: it guides to what is right. They came for an answer and found wonder. That's day six hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Muslims count the jinn among unseen beings with free will; surah al-Jinn and 46:29–32 tell of jinn who heard the Qur'an and believed, and listening to recitation is a devotional practice in its own right.

original.note: Arabic, 72:1: a wondrous recitation. qur'an, recitation; 'ajab, wonder.

trapdoor: what you thought: a strange story about genies.
what it means: unseen beings heard the Qur'an at dawn and were won over by wonder at the recitation itself.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari's Ibn 'Abbas report sets it at Nakhlah; the surah's 'it was revealed to me' fits his view that the Prophet didn't see them.
recall: they didn't say: if God wills

chat.says: What did the jinn say when they heard the Qur'an recited at dawn?
options: That it was wondrous and guides to what is right, so they believed.
That it frightened them, so they fled before the recitation ended.
That it was only poetry, like the verses recited at the market.
chat.meaning: 72:1–2: we have heard a wondrous recitation; it guides to what is right, so we believe in it. Their response was wonder, not fear.

jinn.meaning: unseen beings made from smokeless fire, with free will

Nakhlah.meaning: where the jinn heard the dawn prayer

'Ukaz.meaning: the market the travelers were heading toward

Ibn 'Abbas.meaning: a companion whose report in Bukhari tells the setting

'Between Mecca and Ta'if' for Nakhlah, and the travelers heading to the market of 'Ukaz, follow the hadith; confirm.
